item.title: What developers and QA need from each other when AI writes the code
item.description:
The change was a small edit to a shared component. It passed code review and QA; the tests were green and the code did what the ticket asked.

When a customer purchased a subscription and closed the browser, the system normally turned that order into working access in the background. The change, however, broke that step. An alert from the live system’s logs caught the failure that QA and the code reviewers did not.

The tests weren’t what failed. The handoff was. No one had documented which other services used that component, or in what order they had to change.

Developers’ work and QA’s work come together at the handoff. AI strains that handoff by multiplying changes like this one: small edits to shared code, arriving faster than anyone documents their dependencies.

DORA’s 2025 study of nearly 5,000 technology professionals found that teams adopting AI deliver more while their delivery stability, meaning how often changes fail in production or need unplanned fixes, gets worse.

A green build tells you the code passed its own tests. But those tests were usually written from the same reading of the ticket as the code, so they agree with it by design. A release you can defend to the business needs proof from outside the change, and the handoff decides whether that proof arrives.

Design the handoff before starting delivery

In most delivery teams I work with, the handoff from Development to QA is a ticket changing status and not much else. Architecture, Development, QA and Product all need to agree on the minimum context and evidence that should accompany every change. That agreement becomes the handoff and sign-off contract.

The contract defines what the change should do, in pass-or-fail terms. It names the affected components, dependent services and changed interfaces or data contracts. It lists the open items (unresolved questions, unfinished agent work) and defines the evidence required at each gate and who can accept the residual risk.

During the review, an AI requirements reviewer reads the ticket and checks that the code meets its promises. QA independently assesses whether what the ticket asked for is safe to release, which involves checking whether the specifications were right and whether the system around the change still works.

The communication is reciprocal. QA needs to provide Development with a release signal that differentiates product defects from noise in tests and the environment. QA also needs to call out any missing evidence and say which parts of the handoff helped. That feedback goes into the contract, the test strategy and the automation rules for the next change.

What QA needs from the ticket and from the change

QA has to know what “correct” is before it looks at the code. That comes from the ticket, as approved scope and acceptance criteria that can each be marked pass or fail.

The tests that come with a change usually rest on the same reading of the requirements as the code, so they confirm the code’s own narrative. Take a ticket that states a subscription is canceled at the end of the paid period. QA will write tests based on that statement. If QA instead writes them from the finished code, and the code cancels immediately, those tests confirm that behavior as correct. This is why testing from the requirements should come first.

Then, QA compares two maps. One map shows what the ticket requested, the other what the handoff says was touched. Even if the ticket didn’t mention it, a redeployed shared service belongs on the second map. If dependent services haven’t been updated, or extra work hasn’t been declared, the change is incomplete. Services that are just along for the ride widen the test plan.

Reading the code still matters later for diagnosis, such as stabilizing a test that keeps failing with no product defect behind it.

Match assurance and evidence to the change

Not every change an AI makes requires the same level of proof. Three things make one change much harder to prove than another: whether the code is new or old, how much of the feature the AI generated and how much freedom the tools were given. Real tasks involve a mix of all three.

The easy side is a minor new feature where the engineer still has control of the tools and the quality checks are already in place. The hard side is a major change to an older system that was built with very little supervision, where the context must be rebuilt, so the same change costs more to prove. In that case, proof might require contract tests, integration checks, security or performance evidence and explicit human sign-off.

How much proof you need depends on the business impact and the blast radius, meaning how much else the change can take down. Our small edit showed this when it broke the step that gives a paying customer working access.

Teams collect proof at different checkpoints, like finished tests, completed reviews and checked requirements. The closer you get to release, the higher the bar. And the handoff carries what the next stage would otherwise have to rebuild.

We log each test as a pass or a fail. If a team starts a test but can’t finish it, we mark it as blocked. If we never ran it, we leave it empty. Blocked and empty show where the proof is missing, and so a green build can’t pretend that every test passed.

Measure confidence per unit of time

Confidence per unit of time is how quickly a team can turn a change into a release decision backed by proof. It equals evidence completeness divided by validation lead time, counted only after completeness clears the threshold set for that risk class. Completeness is the share of required evidence items recorded as passed or failed for that risk class, so blocked and empty items don’t count. Validation lead time runs from when a change is ready for review to the recorded release decision. Faster validation is not an improvement if completeness falls.

Take our own change. The build was green, but the checks on the dependent services were empty, which would have meant low completeness and an unfinished release. Empty checks are common. A Tricentis-commissioned 2026 Quality Transformation survey of 2,501 IT and QA professionals found that 60% of organizations report deploying untested code to production.

As changes multiply, raw counts mislead. If your throughput doubles and your escaped defects go up by half, quality improved, even though a raw count reports a regression.

You only need seven signals to get going. Change failure rate stays as it is, and the other six are read as rates or durations. Escaped defect rate is production defects as a share of all defects found. Next comes the share of those escapes rated critical. Validation lead time, defined above, is a segment of DORA’s lead time for changes. The non-product failure rate is test or environment failures as a share of all failures. Sixth is rework on generated code inside a fixed window, such as two weeks after acceptance. Evidence completeness is the one measure with no parent in the standard set, and it uses the four states from the previous section.

Then add two pieces of context: build speed and how often a person has to step in, and make three comparisons: build speed against validation lead time; escaped defects against their severity and change failure rate; rework against non-product failures and human intervention.

Expect a dip at first. DORA’s ROI of AI-assisted software development research describes the early path as a J-curve: a temporary productivity dip and a period of instability while teams pay what it calls a verification tax, the extra time spent reviewing generated code as volume rises.

Start with one delivery path

McKinsey’s 2026 State of AI survey found that nearly three-quarters of AI high performers had fundamentally redesigned workflows, compared with roughly a quarter of other respondents. Redesign doesn’t have to start everywhere. One real delivery path is enough.

Before the next AI-generated change hits that path, the four functions need the handoff and sign-off contract in place. They should measure the handoff against its own baseline and then watch whether checking keeps up with generating. They can give AI tools more freedom only when confidence per unit of time improves and delivery stability holds.

QA is moving from re-running the obvious checks to designing the proof. Development is producing changes the next stage can confirm on its own. Neither role should be evaluated by the number of bugs found.

If you’re accelerating your coding without accelerating your proof, then AI will just help your team reach its next bottleneck faster.

item.description:

The hybrid architecture combines in-memory keys and frequently accessed values with disk-backed storage, reducing garbage-collection overhead and memory consumption.

By Leela Kumili

item.title: AI is changing the build-versus-buy equation. Are CIOs ready?
item.description:
For decades, CIOs have faced a familiar decision when evaluating enterprise software: Should we build it ourselves or buy it from a software provider?

The answer has often favored buying. Commercial software, particularly software as a service (SaaS), provides mature capabilities, ongoing enhancements and technical support. Building custom applications typically requires significant investments in developers, infrastructure, testing, security and maintenance.

Artificial intelligence is beginning to challenge that equation. With AI-powered development tools, applications that once required weeks or months of programming can sometimes be prototyped in hours or days. Developers can generate code, build interfaces and automate testing with less manual effort. Even employees with limited programming experience can describe what they want an application to do and have AI generate a working solution.

This emerging approach, commonly called vibe coding, raises an interesting question for enterprise technology leaders: If AI makes software development faster and less expensive, should we reconsider how much we spend on SaaS applications?

I believe the answer is yes, but with an important qualification. AI is reducing the cost of creating software. It has not eliminated the cost of owning software. The opportunity for CIOs is to reconsider the traditional build-versus-buy decision while recognizing that enterprise software involves far more than generating code.

AI is changing the economics of software development

One of the primary reasons organizations embraced SaaS was the economics of software development. Rather than building and maintaining applications internally, companies could subscribe to established products and benefit from the vendor’s ongoing investments in functionality, security, infrastructure and support.

Over time, however, SaaS portfolios have become increasingly complex. Many enterprises now operate hundreds of applications, some with overlapping capabilities, limited adoption or subscription costs that continue to increase. Business units may purchase specialized tools to address relatively narrow requirements, creating additional integration and governance challenges.

AI-powered development introduces another option. Imagine a department paying an annual subscription for a relatively simple application that manages approvals, tracks requests or coordinates a specialized workflow. Historically, developing a replacement might have required a project team and several months of development. Today, AI-assisted development could make a custom solution economically attractive, particularly if the requirements are straightforward and the organization already has the necessary infrastructure and expertise.

The economics become more interesting when multiplied across an enterprise software portfolio. Replacing selected applications, eliminating overlapping functionality or building targeted capabilities around existing platforms could generate meaningful savings. However, the productivity benefits of AI-assisted development deserve careful examination.

A 2025 randomized controlled study by METR⁠ examined how AI tools affected experienced open-source developers working on familiar codebases. Surprisingly, researchers found that developers using AI tools took approximately 19% longer to complete their assigned tasks, despite expecting the tools to make them faster.

The study focused on a particular development environment and should not be interpreted as evidence that AI generally slows software development. It does, however, illustrate an important point: Generating code faster does not necessarily translate into delivering reliable software faster. CIOs need to evaluate actual development productivity rather than assume that AI automatically produces lower costs.

The hidden costs and risks of replacing SaaS

The excitement surrounding vibe coding is understandable. Watching AI generate a functional application from a few natural-language instructions can make traditional software development appear unnecessarily complicated. But enterprise applications have requirements that extend well beyond whether the software works during a demonstration.

Security is one of the most important considerations. A 2025 report from Veracode examining AI-generated code⁠ found that 45% of the code samples evaluated introduced security vulnerabilities. The research highlights why organizations cannot assume that AI-generated code follows established security practices, even when an application appears functional.

Enterprise applications require authentication, authorization, encryption, vulnerability management and data protection. Depending on their purpose, they may also need to satisfy regulatory, privacy and audit requirements. Those responsibilities remain with the enterprise regardless of how quickly the application was developed.

Maintenance presents another challenge. A SaaS subscription typically includes product enhancements, infrastructure management, patches and technical support. When an organization builds its own application, those responsibilities become internal obligations. Business requirements change, vulnerabilities emerge and integrations break. Applications must be monitored, tested and supported throughout their useful lives. AI may help perform these activities, but it does not eliminate the need for accountability.

This becomes particularly important when applications are created outside traditional IT development teams. Vibe coding can empower non-IT professionals to solve problems without waiting for formal development resources, especially when addressing simple departmental needs. But it can also create a new generation of shadow IT, where applications are deployed without sufficient oversight.

Consider what happens when an employee creates an application that becomes essential to a department’s operations. Who maintains it when the employee leaves? Who ensures that data remains protected and that the application continues functioning when underlying systems change? These questions become more consequential when applications support financial transactions, customer information or other business-critical processes.

Integration is another frequently underestimated cost. A seemingly simple SaaS application may connect to ERP, CRM, identity management and other systems. Replacing it may require rebuilding integrations, migrating data and ensuring that existing workflows continue functioning. An application that works well for a few users may also behave differently when supporting thousands of employees or large transaction volumes.

These considerations reinforce an important distinction: Vibe coding may make software easier to build. It doesn’t necessarily make software easier to own. For CIOs, the relevant measure is total cost of ownership, not simply initial development cost.

Rethinking the build-versus-buy decision

I do not believe AI-powered development means enterprises should begin replacing their major SaaS platforms indiscriminately. Mature ERP, HR, payroll and financial applications contain years of accumulated functionality, business rules and compliance capabilities. Recreating those capabilities internally would introduce significant complexity and risk, even with improvements in development productivity.

The more immediate opportunity may lie in specialized SaaS applications that address relatively narrow, non-critical requirements. Some duplicate capabilities already available in enterprise platforms. Others provide functionality that could potentially be developed internally at a lower long-term cost. These applications deserve another look.

Rather than applying the same build-versus-buy criteria used five years ago, CIOs should evaluate their portfolios through a new lens. I would consider five questions when making these decisions.

  1. Is the capability strategically differentiating? Custom development may provide greater flexibility and control when an application supports a unique business process. Standardized capabilities that offer little differentiation may be better served by commercial products.
  2. How complex is the application? Simple workflows, reporting tools and departmental applications may be good candidates for AI-assisted development. Applications involving complex transactions, regulatory requirements or mission-critical operations require greater scrutiny.
  3. What is the true total cost of ownership? The analysis should include subscription fees, development, infrastructure, integration, security, maintenance and ongoing support. Internal resources required to operate the application must also be considered.
  4. Do we have the capabilities to support what we build? AI may reduce manual programming, but organizations still need architecture standards, secure development practices, testing and operational support. Without these capabilities, technical debt can accumulate quickly.
  5. Can we achieve the same outcome by extending what we already own? Before replacing a SaaS application, organizations should examine whether existing enterprise platforms can provide the required functionality. Many companies are already paying for capabilities they have not fully adopted.

The best alternative to purchasing another SaaS application may not be building a new one. It may be making better use of technology already available.

CIOs should also distinguish between AI-assisted professional development and vibe coding by business users. Professional developers can use AI while applying established engineering practices. Non-IT professionals (AKA users) can create lightweight applications within defined boundaries. Both approaches have value, but they require different levels of governance.

There is another implication worth considering. The same AI capabilities that make custom development more attractive are also available to SaaS providers. Vendors can use AI to accelerate development, automate support and introduce new functionality. As development economics change, CIOs should question whether traditional SaaS pricing models remain appropriate.

If AI reduces the cost of developing and maintaining software, will those efficiencies eventually be reflected in subscription prices? Or will vendors continue increasing prices as they introduce AI features and new licensing models? These questions are worth raising during software renewals and commercial negotiations.

In many cases, the best answer will be a combination of building and buying. Organizations may retain core enterprise platforms while developing targeted applications, workflows and AI agents that extend their functionality. This approach can preserve the stability of established systems while allowing businesses to innovate more quickly.

AI is creating opportunities to simplify application portfolios, reduce unnecessary software spending and develop capabilities that better serve the business. Realizing those benefits requires disciplined evaluation rather than enthusiasm for how quickly software can be generated.

The question is no longer simply whether we can build an application more cheaply than we can buy it. It is whether building, buying or extending existing technology will deliver the best business outcome over the application’s entire life.

That is the decision CIOs need to get right.

item.title: An insider’s look at SAP’s ‘Autonomous Enterprise’
item.description:
At the TechEd developer conference in Berlin, SAP presented additional details of its “Autonomous Enterprise” concept, which includes AI capabilities via Joule Work and SAP Autonomous Suite, built on the SAP Business AI Platform. The company’s focus is not just AI, but AI agents capable of acting automatically within the SAP system by performing analyses and answering queries.

This raises questions, such as: How can the costs of AI agents be controlled? Who is allowed to develop the agents, and how can companies maintain oversight? Jonathan von Rüden, chief AI officer of SAP, explains in an interview with Computerwoche how the software provider is addressing these questions — and where work still needs to be done.

Computerwoche: Companies are increasingly using AI and developing more and more AI agents. But it is often difficult to predict how costs in this area will develop over time. How is SAP addressing this?

Jonathan von Rüden: We generally proceed in three steps. First, we clarify together with the customer or in product management which use cases are relevant and what should be achieved with them.

We distinguish between different areas of focus. First, there’s general productivity: transcriptions, summaries, presentations, or information research. This now extends far beyond classic office tasks. For example, information from the internet can be combined with SAP data and used for financial analysis. However, this area is difficult to define precisely because it encompasses so many tasks in everyday work.

In addition, there are dedicated AI agents that are centrally deployed and managed by IT. These can be standard agents from SAP or customer-specific agents from Joule Studio.

Finally, there are use cases where companies can differentiate themselves significantly. Here, they should consider whether they can develop their own solution.

Based on this information, we estimate consumption. To do this, we consider factors such as the number of employees, how frequently a process is carried out, and how many documents are processed. We also incorporate empirical data from comparable customers and industries.

Ultimately, a large part depends on usage. However, budgets and limits can be set to control costs.

How do these limits prevent costs from spiraling out of control?

In Joule Work, for example, a daily usage limit can be set for each employee. The user can see how much of this limit has already been used via a percentage indicator. Companies can assign different budgets, for example, for individual departments or countries.

If the budget is exhausted, employees can request an additional allocation if, for example, a task absolutely needs to be completed. This allows usage-based billing to be combined with centralized cost control.

The subsequent success measurement is an optional step. Agent and process analysis can be used to verify whether the desired effects have actually materialized.

Many users, as a precaution, opt for the most powerful model — even if it’s the most expensive. How can this be controlled?

The default setting alone has a significant impact. We see this in our own use within SAP: Most people don’t change the default model. If I set a default model that balances costs and performance well, this can already reduce costs considerably.

Companies can therefore consider: Do these employees really always need the most powerful model for their tasks, or is a cheaper one sufficient for everyday use?

Budgets also create an incentive to engage with the issue. If I know that my budget is limited, I’m more likely to consider whether I really need the most expensive model for a particular task.

Couldn’t this selection be made automatically?

We’re working on that with model routers. However, auto-routing is more complex in our use cases than in scenarios where, for example, it’s just about summarizing documents. When a system has to search through and link various transactional business objects, the question of the appropriate model becomes significantly more challenging.

We are currently testing automatic routing internally and plan to make it available to our first customers in the future.

SAP supports 70 LLMs in Joule Work. How much influence do customers generally have on the model selection?

That depends on what they’re building or using. Anyone developing their own agent can choose the model from the available options. In Joule Work, the selection is made via modes like Standard, Extended, or Light; in addition, there’s automatic routing, which we’re currently working on.

We can replace the LLMs behind these modes if a different model is better suited for the respective task. The user then doesn’t have to constantly deal with individual model versions.

For our assistants, the developers decide which models best perform the tasks. They conduct extensive evaluations to determine this. When a new model is released, they check whether it actually improves the assistant. Only then is a replacement worthwhile.

Additionally, we take geographical requirements into account, for example, if customers want to use exclusively European models. In doing so, we must consider regional regulations while simultaneously ensuring that the models offered are suitable for the respective tasks.

What about local models?

For a purely web-based agent, a local model generally plays no role. However, in the desktop application, the models for natural language processing, for example, already run locally. We are working on supporting additional local models.

This is also interesting for users because it allows them to save tokens. For example, they could say: “My token budget is used up, so I’ll continue working with local models.” However, the hardware must be suitable for this. Furthermore, IT departments are often more restrictive when it comes to what can be installed.

On development machines, this is usually not a problem. However, rolling out such solutions on a large scale at a customer’s site is significantly more challenging. We are working on that as well.

Joule Studio makes it relatively easy for non-developers to build agents. How do companies prevent uncontrolled agent proliferation?

First of all, not every user automatically has permission to use Joule Studio. This role is assigned by IT. That’s the first level of control.

At SAP, we’re also initially rolling out Joule Studio to only a few thousand employees outside of IT and development, but not to everyone. We’re starting with those who are already familiar with it and have completed the necessary training. Each company decides on the specific access rules for itself.

Furthermore, not every personal customization needs to result in a company-wide agent. Individual skills can be a first step. This allows you to define, for example, the style in which an agent should deliver results. In this way, I can adapt it to my own workflow.

If something emerges that is also useful for others, I can discuss the next steps with IT: Will I be given permission to develop and share an agent myself? Or should I hand the idea over to a Center of Excellence that will further develop it?

Is there a specific approval process?

In Joule Studio, I can initially share an agent with specific colleagues who can test and work with it. Further access can be controlled via roles and the identity provider. Version control and the ability to later distribute agents to larger user groups are also included.

In the SAP AI Agent Hub, I can see the inventory and the respective status: Which agents need to be reviewed, which have already been reviewed, and which have been rejected.

The lifecycle can also include company-specific approvals. For example, SAP requires approval from the works council before a central agent is rolled out. Similarly, it’s possible to plan when an agent will be decommissioned. The associated IT components are also visible in this process.

How do companies determine whether an agent works reliably and provides value in day-to-day operations?

We combine development, monitoring, and process analysis. This allows us, for example, to analyze the usage and performance of an agent. Connecting to SAP Cloud Application Lifecycle Management enables deeper insights into operational data.

Agent mining and process mining then allow us to examine which decisions the agent makes, which process paths it follows and how often, and how much time each step takes. I can then compare these results with the existing process.

Testing is also part of the process. Tests are automatically generated from the specifications and requirements, which developers can then adapt. The results from testing and operation are fed back into further development.

This creates a cycle: I develop a customization or an agent, share it with others, test its performance, and improve it. Connecting all these components is complex. But for customers, this has a crucial advantage: They don’t have to assemble the individual building blocks from multiple providers.

To ask a somewhat heretical question: Where do you still see gaps?

We’ve made a good start with Financial Operations. Companies can see how many tokens, AI Units, or Agent Actions an agent consumes. We can still improve by directly linking this consumption to the value created.

Because a CFO rightly asks: We’ve spent this amount; what did it bring us? Agent mining can be used to investigate this, but today you need to delve into the analysis in a targeted way.

A more dynamic link between budget and usage would be interesting. For example, if a department currently needs more virtual support, budget could be reallocated there. Budgeting, value comparison, and the connection to the profit and loss statement are areas where there is still considerable potential for development.

Are customers already demanding this transparency?

Yes, we’re getting feedback that we can do more here. However, customers are at different stages. Some don’t yet have the problem of overspending. Others are already at that point.

We ourselves are also investing significantly, which allows us, for example, to work much faster in development. Nevertheless, we need to become even more precise in managing this investment.

Can SAP agents and agents from other providers be managed in an equivalent way?

That depends on what information and interfaces the respective provider offers. There is still no uniform standard for governance and policy enforcement. Currently, this has to be implemented manually. To close this gap, we have announced the SAP Agent Gateway. It simplifies controlled and governance-compliant communication between Joule agents and tools and is available free of charge.

For enterprise-wide runtime control and transparency, there is the SAP Enterprise AI Gateway. It extends the governance functions of the SAP Integration Suite and SAP AI Core and enables the enforcement of policies across all agent interactions.

However, if I want to define more complex rules, I need additional functions. For example, if a transaction exceeds a certain amount, one agent might only be allowed to perform specific actions, while another might not be allowed to take any action at all. The premium functionality of SAP Enterprise AI Gateway is available for defining such policies.

How many agents will companies use in the future? Providers and users alike are currently outdoing each other with the number of AI agents.

You could also call that “agent maxing.” It strongly depends on the definition. For example, if I develop something and Claude Code starts 17 subagents that are active for an hour and then shut down: Do they all count? Then we would probably already be at billions just from our own development.

However, the situation is different when we talk about reusable agents that are permanently available. A rough rule of thumb could be: Let’s take a company that uses roughly a hundred different SaaS applications, whose tasks are initially covered by 10 to 30 agents.

Over time, these agents will become more consolidated. Then, there won’t necessarily be a one-to-one mapping; instead, one agent will take on tasks across multiple applications.

The fundamental business processes remain the same. What changes is how we perform these individual tasks. In the future, they will be handled more extensively by agents or by a combination of agents and other automation solutions.

Are agents always necessary for this? Often, classic automation should suffice.

Absolutely. That’s why Joule Studio also offers the option of building a completely normal, classic workflow with n8n. If a task follows clear rules, a classic workflow is likely to be cheaper and faster.

However, hybrid forms are also possible: For example, I might have 17 workflow steps, but only need additional intelligence in one of them. I would only use an agent for that step. This creates an agent-based workflow that selectively combines classic automation with AI.

This allows me to decide, depending on the use case: Do I need a classic workflow, an agent-based workflow, or a clearly defined agent with access to specific resources? Or do I want an open agent that can utilize the entire knowledge graph and dynamically combine information?

Can specialist users also create such workflows?

I definitely think it makes sense to give these possibilities to specialist users in Joule Studio as well. After all, there are simple processes along the lines of: When a specific email arrives, perform this or that action. Even everyday users can create their own workflows for such tasks — within the rules defined by IT.

What is the next technological step after multi-agent systems?

A trend is already emerging, and initial research results are available: Models are increasingly learning directly how to select and use an agent’s tools — similar to how reasoning abilities were learned about a year and a half ago. This makes the models faster and enables them to make better decisions about which tools to use.

Another very fascinating topic is dynamic learning. The idea is that a model receives feedback and adjusts its own weights accordingly. It actually changes itself. In my estimation, however, research in this area is still in its early stages.

Today, this is often solved using a kind of “second brain”: Information is stored and retrieved as needed. If, however, models could learn directly from feedback, that would, in my view, be a major step towards greater intelligence.

Cybersecurity is also becoming increasingly important. AI is changing both the threat landscape and the possibilities for defense. In my estimation, we will see significantly more specialized models in this area.

And then there are some fascinating approaches, such as that of Yann LeCun, who thinks about how model architectures should work in a completely different way. He sees limits to what LLMs can achieve and therefore pursues other mathematical approaches.

Understanding the world in a different way also means incorporating significantly more data. In a typical business workflow, I might work with 15 tables. That’s a different order of magnitude than a world model — although even that term is defined differently.

LeCun’s approaches, for example, aim to infer missing information in an image or video, rather than predicting the next token. This allows for the inclusion of different and more extensive data because the model doesn’t have to predict every detail, as is the case with a purely autoregressive approach. Which approach is the right one is sometimes debated almost as a matter of faith.

item.title: Why quantum readiness is the next test of global competitiveness
item.description:
The arrival of a quantum computer capable of breaking today’s encryption may still be years away. The business consequences, however, have already begun.

That is the central message of the G7 Cybersecurity Working Group’s new call to action on post-quantum cryptography. The advisory urges organizations to stop treating the quantum threat as a distant technical problem and begin preparing for the transition to encryption designed to withstand attacks from both classical and quantum computers.

This is not simply another compliance exercise for chief information security officers. Post-quantum preparedness is becoming a broader test of business resilience—and, increasingly, a consideration in where multinational companies invest, conduct research and entrust their most sensitive operations.

The quantum threat is already a business risk

The immediate risk is often described as “harvest now, decrypt later.” Malicious actors can collect encrypted information today and retain it until quantum computers become powerful enough to break the public-key cryptography protecting it. That matters for information with a long shelf life: intellectual property, pharmaceutical research, financial records, personal data, trade secrets and sensitive government communications.

A quantum computer capable of breaking today’s public-key encryption does not need to exist today for those assets to be vulnerable. If information must remain confidential for another decade, its exposure window may already have opened.

Preparing for this transition will also be more complex than installing a software patch. Cryptography is embedded throughout modern organizations. It can be found in applications, cloud services, connected devices, identity systems and third-party products. Companies first need to identify where vulnerable cryptography is being used, determine which data requires long-term protection and understand the dependencies running across their supply chains.

The earlier this work begins, the more manageable the transition becomes. Organizations can incorporate quantum-safe technologies into normal procurement and system-renewal cycles rather than undertaking an expensive emergency replacement program later. They can also build crypto-agility: the ability to change cryptographic methods as standards, technologies and threats evolve.

Quantum readiness is becoming a factor in global investment

This has important implications for investment decisions. Multinational companies do not evaluate locations solely on cost, tax or access to customers. They also consider whether a location can protect intellectual property, support regulatory compliance, provide specialized talent and offer reliable digital infrastructure.

In a post-quantum economy, that assessment will increasingly include the maturity of the surrounding cybersecurity ecosystem. Companies will look for markets where public policy, research institutions, technology providers and industry are working together on practical migration challenges. Locations that can support pilot programs, skills development and interoperable standards will be better equipped to attract security-sensitive research, data and operational responsibilities.

Building Ireland’s post-quantum advantage

For Ireland, the G7 advisory is therefore especially relevant. Ireland is a highly digitalized, open economy and a European base for many of the world’s leading technology, financial-services, pharmaceutical and advanced-manufacturing companies. These sectors manage precisely the kinds of valuable and long-lived information that post-quantum cryptography is intended to protect.

Ireland is already laying important groundwork. The National Cyber Security Centre has identified quantum-resistant cryptography as one of its research and innovation priorities. Its agenda raises the practical questions that now need to be answered: which systems should be prioritized, what public-sector use cases require accelerated migration, which pilot programs can validate performance and what skills will be needed to support deployment.

That work complements Quantum 2030, Ireland’s national quantum technologies strategy. The strategy brings together research, talent, international collaboration, innovation and awareness under a common national vision. Ireland’s opportunity is to connect these capabilities with the real operational needs of companies preparing for the post-quantum transition.

That national ambition is increasingly connected to investment across Europe. IrelandQCI, coordinated by the Walton Institute at South East Technological University, is developing quantum communications infrastructure as part of the EU-wide EuroQCI initiative. Jointly funded by Ireland and the EU, the project connects research with practical trials of quantum key distribution. This is a distinct approach to securing communications, alongside the broader need to migrate existing systems to post-quantum cryptography.

The same connection extends to talent and applications. ICHEC, Trinity College Dublin and Walton Institute are participating in the European Quantum Academy to strengthen education and workforce development. ICHEC also represents Ireland in QEX, the European Quantum Excellence Centre supporting quantum computing applications, tools and training. These initiatives give companies investing in Ireland routes into a wider European pool of expertise and research partners.

Ireland will bring that community together when Dublin hosts the European Quantum Technologies Conference from Nov. 30-Dec. 3, 2026, connecting researchers, industry leaders and policymakers. Together, these activities show how investment in domestic capability and participation in Europe’s quantum ecosystem can reinforce one another.

This does not mean positioning Ireland as having already solved the challenge. No country or company has. Standards are evolving, legacy technology remains widespread and migration will require coordination across vendors, industries and borders.

Ireland’s advantage is the interconnectedness of its ecosystem. Global companies, universities, research centers and public agencies operate within a relatively concentrated market, creating opportunities to test approaches across sectors and translate research into deployable solutions.

Post-quantum preparedness could consequently become an important area for research and development investment. Companies will need new security architectures, cryptographic discovery tools, migration services, hardware, software and methods for managing keys and digital identities. They will also need engineers and business leaders who understand both the technical transition and its operational consequences.

Governments can reinforce this through clear national direction, alignment with international standards and public-private partnerships that turn guidance into practical playbooks and testbeds.

Businesses, meanwhile, do not need to wait for perfect certainty. They can begin by taking inventory of their cryptographic assets, evaluating how long sensitive data must remain protected, engaging suppliers and requiring crypto-agility in future technology purchases. The objective is not to replace everything immediately. It is to avoid discovering too late that critical systems cannot adapt.

At IDA Ireland, we are beginning to see a growing number of client companies establish small quantum research teams as part of their wider R&D investments. The new Rinn Quantum Centre, established within the Rinn Network launched in June 2026, is also beginning to explore collaborations with industry across quantum science and technology. Companies can draw on IDA’s R&D support and Rinn Quantum’s research expertise and collaboration opportunities to help develop their quantum research investments. This gives businesses a practical way to build capability now, while connecting their longer-term ambitions to Ireland’s research base and the wider European ecosystem.

The post-quantum transition will unfold over many years, but investment decisions made now will shape which organizations, and which economies, are best prepared. For Ireland, post-quantum readiness is more than a defensive cybersecurity measure. It is an opportunity to demonstrate that resilience, innovation and competitiveness can be built together—and that protecting tomorrow’s economy begins with decisions made today.

item.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: The Future of Apache Iceberg
item.description:
Apache Iceberg V4 proposes a redesign of table metadata to improve scalability and support more frequent writes, alongside new capabilities for data management and schema evolution. Daniel Weeks, co-creator of Apache Iceberg and member of technical staff at Databricks, presented a session at QCon San Francisco on the fourth version of the Apache Iceberg open table format specification.

By Renato Losio

item.title: The leadership gap when technical specialists become executives
item.description:
A successful technical career can prepare someone to lead a function without preparing them to lead everything that comes next. Executive work brings distinct disciplines into the foreground: strategy, interpersonal leadership, business management, consulting and financial judgment. Technical expertise remains valuable, but these capabilities do not emerge automatically from it. They need deliberate development before promotion, not an assumption that the new title will produce them.

Consider a hypothetical programming lead who has spent 30 years writing code and guiding junior developers. That experience can produce excellent technical judgment and valuable mentoring skills. It does not, by itself, demonstrate an ability to choose a business strategy, allocate capital across functions or resolve competing organizational interests. The executive role is not simply the same programming job with more authority. It requires different kinds of judgment.

There are two gaps to assess: executive capability and technical breadth. A cybersecurity specialist moving into a CTO role might inherit responsibility for software engineering, infrastructure, architecture and data systems, depending on the organization. Security expertise does not establish equal depth across those disciplines. The CTO does not need to master every specialty, but needs enough breadth to question specialists, recognize dependencies and make informed trade-offs across their recommendations.

My experience leading enterprise programs across infrastructure, security and transformation is the starting point for how I think about this transition. I believe technical specialists deserve a path into executive leadership. That path should develop the capabilities the next role requires before handing over its authority. I would assess readiness against the decisions candidates will inherit, rather than the years of expertise that earned them consideration.

Laurence J. Peter and Raymond Hull gave this risk a memorable formulation in The Peter Principle: “In a hierarchy, every employee tends to rise to his own level of incompetence.” I would treat that as a warning about promotion decisions, not a verdict on every technical specialist who becomes an executive.

There is research behind that distinction. In Promotions and the Peter Principle, Alan Benson, Danielle Li and Kelly Shue studied sales workers at 131 firms and found that employers favored current performance over other characteristics that better predicted managerial performance. Sales management is not the CIO role. The relevant warning is narrower: success in one job does not establish readiness for another.

Assess readiness against actual decisions

Begin with a practical inventory of the new role. What decisions will land on this executive’s desk in the first six months? Which can they make independently? Where will they need advice, and which areas have they never been responsible for?

Strategy means deciding where the organization will compete, what it will prioritize and what it will stop doing. Business management connects those choices to customers, operating capacity and performance. Consulting skills help an executive diagnose an unfamiliar problem, test how it has been framed and advise stakeholders rather than default to a familiar solution. Interpersonal leadership requires listening, negotiation and influence across people whose expertise and incentives differ from their own.

For financial judgment, the evidence should go beyond delivering a project within budget. Can the candidate challenge a business case, distinguish a cash saving from released capacity and explain what the organization gives up by funding one proposal instead of another? A project can meet its budget and still be the wrong investment.

For people management, look for evidence of developing others and handling performance problems fairly. Being the person who rescues difficult projects is different from creating a team that can deliver without constant intervention. A promotion should not leave everyone waiting for the same expert to resolve every consequential issue.

Organizational design deserves separate attention. Can the leader recognize when a delivery problem comes from unclear ownership, conflicting incentives or insufficient capacity? Replacing a manager or adding a tool will not resolve a structure that makes two teams accountable for incompatible outcomes.

Record each area as demonstrated, supported or untested, with a concrete example behind the assessment. Ask a finance partner, a peer and someone who has reported to the candidate to challenge it. This is a discussion aid, not a scientific score or a reason to disqualify everyone with a gap.

The distinction matters because an untested capability needs a different response from a demonstrated weakness. Someone who has never owned a forecast needs guided exposure. Someone who dismisses financial scrutiny needs to change how they approach the role. Treating both as a generic training need avoids the harder conversation.

Learn enough to own the tradeoff

An executive with a broader mandate cannot become the strongest specialist in every discipline. A more useful goal is to understand enough to test the assumptions, recognize when advice is incomplete and explain the decision to the people affected.

Consider a hypothetical CIO with $2 million available and two proposals. An infrastructure replacement costs $1.2 million. An identity security initiative costs $1 million. Both teams can present credible technical reasons for proceeding. The combined request exceeds the available funding by $200,000.

Choosing whichever proposal sits closest to the CIO’s background would be a poor substitute for analysis. First, establish which obligations are mandatory and which risks can be deferred. The next step is to examine the implementation costs, staffing demands and dependencies, including the cost of operating old and new systems together.

The apparent savings also need scrutiny. If the infrastructure proposal promises to release staff time, when can that capacity be used elsewhere? If it promises lower costs, which payments will actually stop? For the security proposal, what business exposure will be reduced, and how confident is the team in that assessment?

The NIST guidance on integrating cybersecurity with enterprise risk management provides a useful reference. It connects technical risk to enterprise priorities and risk appetite, with accountability and reporting across organizational levels. That supports a conversation about business consequences rather than competing technical preferences.

The answer might be to stage one initiative, reduce its scope or seek additional funding. Require the recommendation to state each option’s consequences, the assumptions that could change the answer and who can accept any remaining risk. An attractive spreadsheet cannot make an unsupported assumption reliable.

Before promoting a specialist with limited financial experience, make this kind of decision part of the development plan. Work through a real investment proposal with finance. Revisit its forecast after implementation. Explain the variance. That creates evidence of learning that a course completion alone cannot provide.

Apply the same approach to people leadership through supervised experience with hiring, coaching and performance decisions. Give candidates exposure to strategy and business management before they assume full responsibility for them. Development should continue after promotion, but it should not begin there.

Build a team that can challenge your judgment

A capability assessment should influence the team around the executive. A leader with deep infrastructure expertise may need a strong security counterpart, a finance partner who challenges assumptions or an operations leader who understands how changes affect customers. The right combination depends on the mandate and the gaps identified.

I am wary of treating a team full of familiar expertise as a sign of readiness. Agreement is easier when everyone starts with the same assumptions. A complementary team should improve the questions being asked, especially where the executive’s own knowledge is thin.

That requires more than inviting people to meetings. For a consequential decision, identify who recommends an option, who must be consulted and who makes the final call. Also make clear which decisions managers can take without escalation. Otherwise, adding experts can create another layer of approval while leaving the executive as the bottleneck.

The leader’s behavior determines whether those experts contribute their real judgment. Amy Edmondson’s study of psychological safety and learning in work teams examined 51 work teams in a manufacturing company and found an association between psychological safety and learning behavior. That finding does not guarantee better executive decisions, but it gives leaders a reason to take the interpersonal cost of speaking up seriously.

Make disagreement specific. What evidence contradicts the preferred option? Which assumption is weakest? What would cause us to stop or change course? The executive should be willing to answer those questions about their own recommendation before expecting candor from everyone else.

Accountability remains essential. Consultation should end in a decision, with an owner and a date to review what happened. When new evidence changes the answer, the leader should explain the revision rather than quietly rewriting the original rationale. Teams need to see that raising a concern can affect the outcome.

For a newly promoted specialist, I would judge progress by the quality of decisions beyond their original discipline and by the judgment developing in the people around them. Can they defend an investment in business terms? Can their managers act within clear boundaries? Are important gaps becoming visible early enough to address?

Technical expertise earns trust for good reasons. Executive leadership requires extending that trust into areas where personal expertise has limits. I would rather see a leader name those limits, build the right support and remain accountable than pretend the promotion has made the gaps disappear.

item.title: AWS Releases a Free Local Emulator of AWS Built Entirely by Agents
item.description:
AWS has released AWS Emulator, a free, CC0-licensed local stand-in for more than 200 of its services, generated from its public API models and aimed at the test loops of coding agents. AWS says agents wrote and maintain all of the code and publishes per-release fidelity scores. The docs say it does not evaluate IAM, and practitioners are split on trusting an emulator nobody reviewed.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers
